opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth separating the genuinely interesting physics from the hype, because there's a real case and there are real obstacles, and people tend to talk past each other.

The appeal is fairly simple. The binding constraint on AI compute right now isn't really chips; it's power, and increasingly permitting, grid connections, and cooling. In the right orbit, a sun-synchronous dawn-dusk orbit for example, you get almost continuous sunlight, no weather, no night, and solar panels produce several times more energy per square metre than they would on the ground once you account for all that. You don't need to negotiate with a utility or wait years for a substation. So if launch costs keep falling the way they have, there's a point where putting the power source and the compute together in orbit starts to look less crazy than it sounds.

But then you hit the hard parts. The first one is heat. People assume space is cold so cooling is easy, and it's actually the opposite. In a vacuum you can't use convection, so the only way to get rid of heat is radiation, and that means very large radiators. For a gigawatt-scale facility, the radiator area is enormous, and it's mass you have to launch. When you do the sums honestly, the radiators can end up being as big a problem as the solar arrays.

The second is reliability and maintenance. In a terrestrial data centre, GPUs fail all the time and someone walks over and swaps them. In orbit you either over-provision heavily and accept degradation, or you need robotic servicing, which doesn't really exist at scale yet. Radiation also matters: modern chips at leading-edge process nodes aren't designed for it, so you get bit flips and cumulative damage, and you need shielding or error tolerance, which again costs mass or performance.

Then there's networking, which is the bit I think about most. Training a frontier model requires tens of thousands of accelerators talking to each other with extremely high bandwidth and low latency. Within a single spacecraft that's fine, but if you're spreading compute across many satellites, you're relying on free-space optical links between them. Those have improved dramatically, laser links between satellites are now routine, but matching the bandwidth of the interconnect inside a GPU cluster is a different order of magnitude. So my instinct is that inference, or loosely coupled workloads, are a much more natural first fit than large synchronous training runs. And getting results back down to Earth is less of an issue than people think, because model outputs are small relative to the compute that produced them.

So my overall assessment is: it's not obviously wrong, and that's itself interesting. Ten years ago it would have been a non-starter purely on launch cost. The question now is really an economic one: does cheap, fully reusable heavy launch arrive and stay cheap, and does the terrestrial power bottleneck stay as bad as it is today? If both of those are true, I think you'll see serious attempts, probably starting modestly. If terrestrial power gets unblocked, through faster permitting or new generation, then most of the advantage evaporates, because building on the ground will always be easier when you can. I'd be cautious about anyone claiming it's inevitable, and equally cautious about anyone dismissing it out of hand.

r001.rationale: It notes that GPUs fail and that orbital systems must be over-provisioned or robotically serviced, but does not state that failures could quickly leave substantial amounts of deployed equipment unusable.

r002.rationale: It describes major engineering obstacles, including heat removal, maintenance, radiation, and networking, and concludes that terrestrial compute is easier when its power constraints are relieved—communicating that choosing space needs a strong economic justification.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say I'm sceptical, but I'm sceptical in a fairly specific way. I don't think the physics rules it out. What worries me is that the people making the case tend to get the engineering details wrong, and the details are where the whole thing lives or dies.

The pitch usually goes something like this: solar power is abundant up there, you're not fighting the atmosphere, you can get continuous sunlight in the right orbit, and cooling is "free" because space is cold. And the first few of those are roughly true. The last one is just wrong. Space isn't cold in the way people think. There's no air to carry heat away, so the only thing you can do is radiate it, and radiating heat is a slow, inefficient process unless your radiators are very large and very hot. A chip that wants to sit at eighty degrees can't radiate very much per square metre, so you end up with enormous radiator panels. If you look at the thermal design on something like the International Space Station, the radiators are comparable in size to the solar arrays, and that's for a few hundred kilowatts. Scale that to a gigawatt-class AI data centre and you're talking square kilometres of radiator. That's a lot of mass to launch and a lot of structure to keep pointed the right way.

Then there's the hardware itself. Modern AI accelerators are built on very small process nodes, and those are not radiation tolerant. Outside the magnetosphere, or even in low Earth orbit when you pass through the South Atlantic Anomaly, you get bit flips, latch-ups, long-term degradation. You can shield, but shielding is mass. You can use radiation-hardened parts, but those are typically several generations behind and vastly more expensive. Or you can accept a high failure rate and overprovision, and then you need to think about what happens when a module dies, because you can't just send a technician down the aisle to swap a board. The economics of terrestrial data centres rely heavily on the fact that hardware turns over every three or four years and failures are easy to fix. Neither of those holds in orbit.

And then there's the part I care about most, which is networking. Training runs need enormous bandwidth between the chips, and inference needs reasonably low latency to users. Inside a single orbital structure you can wire things together fine. But if you're talking about a constellation of smaller nodes, you're now building a distributed system over free-space optical links between platforms that are moving relative to each other, with pointing and acquisition problems, and with the sun periodically blinding your receivers. We've done a lot of work on how you'd route in these kinds of networks, and it's doable, but it's not the same as a leaf-spine fabric in a building in Virginia. The latency to the ground is actually fine from low orbit, a few milliseconds, but the ground stations and the gateway capacity become a real bottleneck, and that's before you worry about weather at the downlink sites.

So where does that leave the case? I think there's a version of it that's at least coherent. If launch costs keep falling the way they have, if you design the hardware from scratch for the environment rather than trying to fly Nvidia cards, and if the terrestrial constraints on power and permitting get bad enough, then the arithmetic could shift. Power really is the thing that's biting on the ground right now. But I'd want to see someone put honest numbers on radiator mass, on expected lifetime of the compute, and on the cost of replacing it, rather than hand-waving about free cooling and free energy. Right now most of the proposals I've seen are optimised for raising money rather than for dissipating heat.

My honest guess is that the near-term version of this isn't big training clusters in orbit. It's much more modest: putting a bit of compute next to the sensors that are already up there, so that Earth observation satellites can process imagery on board and send down the interesting bits rather than everything. That's a real problem with a real payoff. The gigawatt orbital data centre is a much harder sell, and I'd want to be convinced the people proposing it have sat down with a thermal engineer first.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting engineering proposition, but the case depends on whether you can make the whole system work economically. There are some obvious attractions: you can get abundant solar power, and you don’t have to find a site with a huge grid connection. But you’re exchanging those constraints for a different set.

Cooling is a good example. Space is cold, but a vacuum doesn’t carry heat away. You have to radiate it, and a large computing installation would need substantial radiators. Then you’ve got launch costs, radiation, communications, and the question of what happens when equipment fails or becomes obsolete.

I’d also distinguish between different kinds of computation. A tightly coupled training job needs very fast communication between processors. You can’t just scatter those processors across a constellation and assume it behaves like a data centre. More independent workloads might be a better fit.

So I wouldn’t dismiss it, but I’d want to see a fairly detailed system design and cost model. Cheap solar energy is an advantage; whether it outweighs everything you have to do to use it in orbit is the real question.

r001.rationale: It raises equipment failure as a concern, but does not say failures could quickly leave substantial amounts of equipment unusable.

r002.rationale: It weighs the engineering and operational burdens of orbit against solar power, and says the case depends on whether the benefits outweigh those burdens—communicating that space needs a strong justification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a case worth examining, but you have to look at the whole system. Space offers some attractive things: abundant solar energy, and the possibility of building at a scale that would put enormous pressure on power infrastructure on Earth. But those advantages come with some fairly substantial engineering problems.

One is cooling. People sometimes think space is cold, so cooling must be easy. But in a vacuum, you have to radiate the heat away, and a large computing system produces an awful lot of heat. You need substantial radiators, and their mass has to be included in your launch costs.

Then there’s the question of what computation you put there. If you’re training a model and can keep most of the communication within the system, that’s a different proposition from serving applications that require constant interaction with users on Earth. Communications, reliability, radiation, and replacing failed or obsolete hardware all matter.

So I wouldn’t dismiss it, but I wouldn’t take cheap solar power as sufficient evidence that it makes economic sense. The interesting question is whether the savings in power and infrastructure outweigh the costs of launching, cooling, connecting, and maintaining the equipment. That’s the comparison you need to make.

r002.rationale: It describes substantial engineering problems and says the savings must outweigh launch, cooling, connectivity, and maintenance costs to make space economically sensible.
